title: AI models built outside the US and China are nearly a year behind
content:
AI models built outside the US and China are nearly a year behind
Since 2024, the best AI models from labs outside the US and China have arrived about 10 months after American ones reached the same level, nearly twice China’s lag. Mistral and South Korea are closing some of that gap; Cohere and the UAE have fallen further behind.
Countries outside the US and China want AI labs of their own, an idea often called sovereign AI. France has Mistral, Canada has Cohere, the UAE has the government-funded Technology Innovation Institute, South Korea has half a dozen labs building Korean models, and India’s national AI mission supplies the compute for Sarvam AI. Village’s LLM Atlas puts 857 models on one capability scale estimated from hundreds of public benchmarks, which lets us measure how far behind each of them is. Since 2024, the best of them have trailed the US by nearly a year.
Everyone else trails by nearly a year
- About 10 months behind the US. Since 2024, each new best model from outside the US and China has arrived a median of 9.9 months after a US model reached the same score, and never less than 7.3 months after.
- Nearly twice China’s gap. New Chinese records have arrived a median of 5.2 months behind.
- They release far fewer models. Labs outside the two countries released about 20 of the models Atlas ranks from 2026, against 113 from the US and 79 from China.
Sovereign labs are not falling further behind, but they are not catching up either. They have stayed in a band about a year back, while China runs about half that distance behind the US.
Country by country
- South Korea and Mistral run closest to the US. Their new records have landed about 10 months behind.
- India is furthest behind. Sarvam AI’s best model, Sarvam 30B from March, scores where US models were 28 months earlier.
Those medians cover two years in which most of these efforts changed course, and since then their gaps have moved in opposite directions.
Their strategies are diverging
- Mistral went back to open-weight flagships. After a 2025 in which its best models were closed, it released Mistral Large 4’s weights in October and pitched it as Europe’s answer to China’s open models. That cut its gap to about 8 months.
- South Korea is closing in. A government program funds rival labs to build national models and narrows the field each round, and Korea’s gap has roughly halved since 2024. Its best model, Motif-3-Beta, came from a team the program dropped in August despite the top benchmark score.
- Cohere bet on enterprise software. It now sells North, an agent platform that also runs other companies’ models, and in April agreed to buy Germany’s Aleph Alpha. Its own models have slipped to about 18 months behind.
- The UAE is building compute more than models. Its flagship project is Stargate UAE, a data-center campus built with OpenAI. MBZUAI’s K2 Think V2, the country’s best model, sits more than 16 months behind.
- India moved from fine-tuning to training its own. Sarvam’s first model adapted Mistral Small; Sarvam 30B and 105B, trained from scratch on government-funded GPUs, land further behind.
The two efforts closing in are still training large general-purpose models of their own. The others have put more into platforms, data centers or national-language models, which a general capability score rewards less.
How we built this
This study uses Village’s LLM Atlas, which estimates one capability score per model from public benchmark results with a Bayesian item-response model, described in its methodology. Labs are assigned to the country of their headquarters. Months behind measures how long before a model’s release a US model first reached the same score, at each new best model for a country or lab since 2024; Atlas covers few models from before 2023, so early-2024 gaps rest on thinner comparisons. Cohere’s Command R, from March 2024, is 23 months behind only because DeepMind’s Chinchilla reached its score in 2022. The scores are from October 31, 2026; Atlas updates as new results arrive.
We leave out two models built on other labs’ work that would otherwise lead everyone outside the US and China: Sakana AI’s Fugu Ultra, an orchestrator that routes questions through other labs’ models, and Mind Lab’s Macaron-V1-Venti, which adds fine-tuned specialists to Zhipu’s Chinese GLM-5.2. Restricting to models scored on at least 10 benchmark families gives the same order and similar gaps, though it drops Sarvam, none of whose models has that many. Atlas’s benchmarks are mostly in English, which may understate models built for Korean, Arabic, Indian or other languages. India’s figure rests on two Sarvam models. Mistral Large 4’s weights came out on October 29.

report.summary: Village's LLM Atlas finds the best AI models from labs outside the US and China trail American frontier models by a median of roughly 10 months — nearly double China's lag.
report.background: Since 2024, governments from Paris to Seoul to Abu Dhabi have poured money into "sovereign AI" — the belief that a country needs its own frontier models rather than renting American or Chinese ones. France has Mistral, Canada has Cohere, South Korea funds a national lab program, the UAE backs the Technology Innovation Institute and MBZUAI, and India's AI mission supplies GPUs to Sarvam AI. Until now, though, there was no common yardstick to say how far behind these efforts actually were. Village's LLM Atlas attempts to fix that by scoring 857 models on a single capability scale, estimated from hundreds of public benchmark results using a Bayesian item-response model, then measuring how long before each model's release a US model first hit the same score. The result is a rare quantitative look at whether sovereign AI is closing the gap or merely standing still.
key_points: About 10 months behind: since 2024, each new best model from outside the US and China has arrived a median of 9.9 months after a US model reached the same capability score, and never sooner than 7.3 months. The lag is remarkably stable rather than shrinking.

China moves twice as fast: new Chinese records arrive a median of 5.2 months behind the US, roughly half the gap of everyone else. Labs outside the two superpowers also released far fewer models — about 20 ranked in 2026 versus 113 from the US and 79 from China.

Strategies are diverging. Mistral returned to open-weight flagships with Mistral Large 4 in October, cutting its gap to roughly 8 months, while South Korea's state program has halved its lag since 2024. Cohere pivoted to enterprise agent software and slipped to about 18 months behind.

Compute over models: the UAE's flagship effort is Stargate UAE, a data-center campus built with OpenAI, and its best model sits more than 16 months back. India's Sarvam moved from fine-tuning Mistral to training from scratch, but its best model scores where US models were 28 months earlier — the furthest behind of any country studied.

Methodology caveats: Atlas benchmarks are mostly English, which likely understates Korean, Arabic and Indic models, and the study excludes orchestrators and fine-tunes built on other labs' models (Sakana's Fugu Ultra, Mind Lab's Macaron) that would otherwise lead the pack.
report.impact: The finding reframes the sovereign-AI debate: national labs are not collapsing, but they are not converging either, stuck in a stable one-year band while China runs at half that distance. For the industry, it suggests frontier capability will stay a two-country game, and that challengers should compete on distribution, enterprise integration, cost or language coverage rather than raw benchmark scores. For developers, the practical takeaway is to treat non-US/China models as a deliberate trade-off — a capability discount in exchange for data residency, local-language quality or price — and to benchmark on their own tasks rather than trusting a global score. For regular users, especially outside English-speaking markets, the upside is more choice in their own language; the risk is that critical AI infrastructure remains dependent on foreign labs and foreign policy.
report.tools: To follow up, explore Village's LLM Atlas (village.dev), which publishes the capability scale and methodology and updates as new results arrive. For hands-on comparison, try Mistral Large 4's released open weights, Sarvam AI's 30B and 105B models, South Korea's Motif-3-Beta, and MBZUAI's K2 Think V2. Cohere's North agent platform and Germany's Aleph Alpha (being acquired by Cohere) are worth watching for the enterprise-software route. Standard open-weight hubs and evaluation harnesses such as Hugging Face and lm-evaluation-harness let you re-run benchmarks on your own workload.
